# Paired cards for checking a fictional sorting procedure

DOI: 10.99999/synthetic.research-paper.1

Synthetic methods paper for workflow testing. No real authors, observations,
data or research results are represented. All examples and outcomes below are
invented; this document is not scientific evidence.

## Abstract

[1] We describe a fictional procedure for checking whether a sorting instruction
can be followed consistently when irrelevant card decorations change. The method
pairs cards that share a target shape but differ in border style. Its purpose is
to separate errors in an instruction from errors introduced by presentation. In
the invented demonstration, disagreement between paired decisions reveals an
ambiguous tie rule. The example illustrates a possible diagnostic, not an estimate
of performance in any population. A paired comparison may help locate ambiguity,
but it cannot establish that the target categories are useful.

## Introduction

[2] A sorting instruction often combines a category definition with a sequence
of decisions. A reader can misunderstand either part. Repeating the same card
shows whether an answer is stable, while changing a decoration asks a different
question: whether a feature declared irrelevant changes the answer. These checks
can disagree without contradiction. A stable answer can follow the wrong rule,
and an unstable answer can reflect an instruction that permits several readings.
The present example concerns only the second possibility.

[3] We propose paired cards as a transparent way to inspect that ambiguity.
Each pair preserves the feature named by the instruction and changes one feature
that the instruction excludes. The comparison requires a written account of which
features matter. Without that account, disagreement cannot identify a violation.
The fictional exercise deliberately uses simple shapes so that the decision path
can be inspected without specialist knowledge or external reference material.

## Methods

[4] A fictional deck contains circles and triangles drawn inside plain or dotted
borders. The instruction assigns a card to the first tray when its central shape
has three corners and to the second tray otherwise. A separate sentence says
that borders do not affect assignment. For each central shape, the demonstrator
prepares one plain-border card and one dotted-border card. Card order is reversed
for a second pass. The demonstrator records the chosen tray and a short reason
before revealing the pairing. These are proposed steps, not an account of an
experiment that actually took place.

[5] The diagnostic compares reasons as well as tray choices. Matching choices
with incompatible reasons do not count as evidence that the instruction was
understood. Differing choices prompt inspection of the exact decision sentence.
A deliberately ambiguous practice card contains an incomplete triangle. The
instruction does not specify whether an interrupted outline has three corners.
The demonstrator retains both interpretations instead of silently deciding which
one is correct. No statistical agreement measure is computed.

## Results

[6] In the invented walkthrough, complete triangles reach the first tray under
both border styles. The incomplete practice card receives different assignments
on the two passes. The recorded reasons attribute this difference to counting
visible corners versus completing the outline mentally. Rewriting the instruction
to name visible corners removes that ambiguity within the example. This narrated
outcome is a constructed teaching case. It supplies no measured error rate, sample
size, validation result or evidence about actual readers.

## Discussion

[7] Paired presentation can expose a dependency that the instruction intended
to exclude. It does not by itself identify the best category definition or prove
that a revised rule will generalize. Changes to both shape and border would make
the comparison harder to interpret. The method therefore depends on preserving
the target feature across each pair and documenting the intended invariance.
Future real evaluation would require independently prepared cards, explicit
scoring rules and readers who had not helped draft the instruction. Until then,
this fictional example supports only discussion of the proposed checking method.
